title: Ἑρμῆς καὶ γῆ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 109 (= Perry 102). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ζεὺς πλάσας ἄνδρα καὶ γυναῖκα ἐκέλευσεν Ἑρμῆν ἀγαγεῖν αὐτοὺς ἐπὶ τὴν Γῆν καὶ δεῖξαι ὅθεν ὀρύσσοντες τροφὴν ἑαυτοῖς πορίσουσι.
sentences.tr: Zeus plasas andra kai gynaika ekeleusen Hermēn agagein autous epi tēn Gēn kai deixai hothen oryssontes trophēn heautois porisousi.
sentences.l: Zeus, having moulded a man and a woman, ordered Hermes to lead them to the Earth and to show them whence, by digging, they will provide food for themselves.
sentences.i: Zeus, when he had moulded man and woman, bade Hermes lead them out to the Earth and show them where they might dig and so get themselves food.
sentences.n: πλάσας, from πλάσσω, is the potter's word for moulding clay, and the standard verb for a god's making of men. ὅθεν … πορίσουσι keeps the future indicative inside the indirect question, as Greek regularly does even after a past main verb. ὀρύσσοντες is a participle of means: the food comes by digging.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ τὸ προσταχθὲν ποιήσαντος, ἡ Γῆ τὸ μὲν πρῶτον ἐκώλυεν.
sentences.tr: Tou de to prostachthen poiēsantos, hē Gē to men prōton ekōlyen.
sentences.l: And he having done the thing ordered, the Earth at first tried to prevent it.
sentences.i: And when he had done as he was told, the Earth at first would not allow it.
sentences.n: τὸ προσταχθέν is the aorist passive participle used as a noun, 'the thing that had been ordered'. τὸ μὲν πρῶτον is adverbial, 'at first', and its μέν announces the ὡς δέ of the next sentence. ἐκώλυεν is the imperfect of attempted action: she set about hindering, and did not succeed.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ Ἑρμῆς ἠνάγκαζε λέγων τὸν Δία προστεταχέναι, ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ὀρυσσέτωσαν ὅσον βούλονται· στένοντες γὰρ αὐτὸ καὶ κλαίοντες ἀποδώσουσι. »
sentences.tr: Hōs de Hermēs ēnankaze legōn ton Dia prostetachenai, ephē· « All’ oryssetōsan hoson boulontai· stenontes gar auto kai klaiontes apodōsousi. »
sentences.l: But when Hermes kept compelling her, saying that Zeus had ordered it, she said: « Well, let them dig as much as they wish; for groaning and weeping they will pay it back. »
sentences.i: But when Hermes pressed her, saying that this was Zeus's own command, she said: « Very well, let them dig as much as they please; they will pay it back with groans and tears. »
sentences.n: τὸν Δία προστεταχέναι is the accusative and infinitive of indirect statement after λέγων: the subject of the reported words goes into the accusative and its verb into the infinitive. ὀρυσσέτωσαν is a third-person imperative, Greek's way of saying 'let them dig'. αὐτό is neuter and matches none of the feminine nouns before it; it points loosely at what they take out of her — the loan, which is the fable's real subject.

sentences.t: Πρὸς τοὺς ῥᾳδίως δανειζομένους, μετὰ λύπης δὲ ἀποδιδόντας ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros tous rhāidiōs daneizomenous, meta lypēs de apodidontas ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against those who borrow readily, but pay back with grief, the story is well-timed.
sentences.i: The story is well aimed at those who borrow lightly and repay in sorrow.
sentences.n: δανείζομαι in the middle is to have money lent to one, that is, to borrow; the active δανείζω is to lend. No μέν is written, but the δέ after μετὰ λύπης sets the ease of the borrowing against the grief of the paying back. The Earth is the creditor and men's food the loan.
